title: Kaiyue Wen (@wen_kaiyue) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] (1/n) Check out our new paper: "Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them"! >4000 models to find the fastest optimizer! 2× speedups over AdamW? Unlikely. Beware under-tuned baseline or limited scale! E.g. Muon: ~40% speedups <0.5B & only 10% at 1.2B (8× Chinchilla)!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A44SebkAA6Gux.jpg
────────
[2/13] (2/n) AdamW has ruled LLM pretraining forever, despite papers claiming 1.4-2x faster alternatives. But why was there no widespread adoption until Muon? We dug in: two big issues obscure fair comparisons.
First Issue: Unequal hyperparameter tuning.
(i) Baselines often undertuned! Tuning JUST the LR in the commonly used AdamW baseline gives 2x speedup on 130M models.
(ii) Fixing shared hyperparameters does not guarantee fair comparison, e.g. Lion prefers high wd (0.6) compared to the standard weight decay 0.1
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A4-wXbkAIqPO-.jpg
────────
[3/13] (3/n) Second issue: Lack of scale. Most tests use only small models (<<1B) or 1x Chinchilla data ratio. What about bigger scales or a higher data ratio? Early checkpoints can be misleading too—loss curves cross during LR decay, flipping rankings. Need end-of-training evals across regimes!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5DW0bkAAUY2j.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5FXPagAAR7G5.png
────────
[4/13] (5/n) New insights on design: Matrix-based optimizers consistently outperform scalar-based optimizers!
Scalar-based opts (AdamW, Lion, Mars, etc.) reach similar speed (<1.2x speedup) over AdamW. Matrix-based (Muon, Soap, Kron) win consistently: ~1.3x on <520M, using matrix preconditioners on gradients. However, this gain diminishes to only 1.1x to 1.2B models (more on this later)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5hljbkAIDV2u.png
────────
[5/13] (4/n) Our setup: Benchmarked 11 opts (AdamW, NAdamW, Lion, Sophia, Mars, Cautious, Adam-mini, Muon, Scion, Kron, Soap) on Llama-style models: 130M-1.2B params with rigorous 3-phase approach.
Phase I: Per-hyperparameter coordinate descent on 130M (1-8x Chinchilla) and 300M, 520M (1x Chinchilla) -> Identify scale-sensitive hyperparameters that (i) change with scales and (ii) critically influence the loss
Phase II: Coordinate descent on 300M, 520M (2-8x Chinchilla) on scale-sensitive hyperparameters
Phase III: Extrapolate hyperparameter scaling laws to 1.2B (fit power laws to HPs like LR).
No shortcuts—fair for ALL optimizers.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5eI_bkAIb36i.jpg
────────
[6/13] (6/n) New insights on design: Variance-reduction techniques provide a small but clear lift. Within the scalar-based family, all variance-reduced Adam variants (NAdamW, Mars, Cautious) consistently surpass vanilla AdamW with a consistent 1.1x speedup.
────────
[7/13] (8/n) See more results in our papers, including (i) common optimization phenomenon across different optimizers; (ii) different scaling behavior for memory-efficient Adam replacement: Adam-mini improves with scale, and Lion worsens.
────────
[8/13] (7/n) Room for improvement: the best optimizers differ across scaling regimes & speedup diminishes with respect to the model scale.
(i) Muon is best at low Chinchilla ratios, but Kron/Soap pulls ahead at 8x Chinchilla
(ii) Muon, Soap, and NAdamW all converge to 1.1x Speedup in the largest experiment (1.2B 8x Chinchilla)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5u5db0AApQ1K.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0A5v5BbkAMde5W.png
────────
[9/13] (10/n) Their initial tuning on small batches (~0.1M tokens, 1-8x H100s) favors variance reduction in noisy regimes. Our Phase I: Larger batches (~0.4M, 128 TPU v5s) reduce noise, making matrix preconditioning shine. In their scale-up experiments (720M, 1M batch size), we have closer alignment, but tuning varies (our higher LRs, separate Embed lr tuning). Key: Benchmarks sensitive to setup—context matters! 🚀
────────
[10/13] (9/n) Amazing concurrent work [2509.01440] Benchmarking Optimizers for Large Language Model Pretraining (Semenov et al.) also shows the speedup effect of variance-reduced optimizers, and our benchmarking results share the same spirit of rigorous tuning!
But diffs: We see matrix-based opts (Muon, Soap, Kron) outperform even tuned variance-reduced baselines; they find AdEMaMix/Mars beat Muon. Why? We hypothesize it is due to discrepancies in batch size!
────────
[11/13] (11/n) Our work would not have been possible without the Marin project ( and Google TRC compute, and we invite everyone interested in speeding up pretraining even further to participate in our Speedrun (
────────
[12/13] (11/n) Why care? Pretraining is still costly, and even 1.1-1.3x savings matter at scale. But no silver bullet (yet)! Careful tuning in a proper setting is still required to fully unleash the benefit of modern optimizers over AdamW. We hope to see even more algorithmic improvement in the optimizer space, from better hyperparameter transfer across scales to more effective update rules, to extend the 1.3-1.4x speedups to even larger models.
────────

title: Kaiyue Wen (@wen_kaiyue) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] (1/n) Introducing Hyperball — an optimizer wrapper that keeps weight & update norm constant and lets you control the effective (angular) step size directly. Result: sustained speedups across scales + strong hyperparameter transfer.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NWq06aIAAV_ZC.jpg
────────
[2/7] (2/n) Hyperball leads to empirical speedup while keeping a constant weight norm and virtually 0 step-wise overhead. ✨Blog:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NWvVgbYAA-2bU.png
────────
[3/7] (3/n) As a by-product of the constant ratio between update and weight norm, we observe a consistent learning rate scaling (especially depth wise)!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NWzK9XkAAkZNg.jpg
────────
[4/7] (4/n) We explored a scaled up 8B 1x Chinchilla experiment ( with the Adam recipe used in Marin 8B and found a shocking 0.04 loss reduction! @WilliamBarrHeld performed the run and this is our first ferry run in Marin.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NW4BPXgAA7cmH.jpg
────────
[5/7] (6/n) Why not weight-decay (WD)? In mostly scale-invariant networks (e.g., LMs), learning speed is set by how fast weight directions change, not norms. WD softly controls norms and thus imposes a suboptimal direction schedule. Hyperball decouples them explicitly.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NXAYAaIAAIcrJ.jpg
────────
[6/7] (5/n) Will normalized weights hurt representation power? Fortunately, this isn't the case for architectures that use RMSNorm with rescaling parameters. These parameters now steer the norm of the output when the weight norm is fixed as a constant.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_NW8fWaIAUneun.jpg
────────

title: Kaiyue Wen (@wen_kaiyue)
summary:
I’ve had the privilege of testing OA. The unlinkable inference layer ensures that responses are no longer influenced by past interactions, which often leads to a more neutral and unbiased perspective!
Quoting @kenziyuliu
Can we build a blind, *unlinkable inference* layer where ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini can't tell which call came from which users, like a “VPN for AI inference”?
Yes! Blog post below + we built it into open source infra/chat app and served >15k prompts at Stanford so far. How it helps with AI user privacy:
# The AI user privacy problem
If you ask AI to analyze your ChatGPT history today, it’s surprisingly easy to infer your demographics, health, immigration status, and political beliefs. Every prompt we send accumulates into an (identity-linked) profile that the AI lab controls completely and indefinitely. At a minimum this is a goldmine for ads (as we know now). A bigger issue is the concentration of power: AI labs can easily become (or asked to become) a Cambridge Analytica, whistleblow your immigration status, or work with health insurance to adjust your premium if they so choose.
This is a uniquely worse problem than search engines because your average query is now more revealing (not just keywords), interactive, and intelligence is now cheap. Despite this, most of us still want these remote models; they’re just too good and convenient! (this is aka the "privacy paradox".)
# Unlinkable inference as a user privacy architecture
The idea of unlinkable inference is to add privacy while preserving access to the remote models controlled by someone else. A “privacy wrapper” or “VPN for AI inference”, so to speak.
Concretely, it’s a blind inference middle layer that:
(1) consists of decentralized proxies that anyone can operate;
(2) blindly authenticates requests (via blind signatures / RFC9474,9578) so requests are provably sandboxed from each other and from user identity;
(3) relays prompts over randomly chosen proxies that don’t see or log traffic (via client-side ephemeral keys or hosting in TEEs); and
(4) the provider simply sees a mixed pool of anonymous prompts from the proxies. No state, pseudonyms, or linkable metadata.
If you squint, an unlinkable inference layer is essentially a vendor for per-request, anonymous, ephemeral AI access credentials (for users or agents alike). It partitions your context so that user tracking is drastically harder.
Obviously, unlinkability isn’t a silver bullet: the prompt itself still goes to the remote model and can leak privacy (so don't use our chat app for a therapy session!). It aims to combat *longitudinal tracking* as a major threat to user privacy, and its statistical power increases quickly by mixing more users and requests.
Unlinkability can be applied at any granularity. For an AI chat app, you can unlinkably request a fresh ephemeral key for every session so tracking is virtually impossible.
# The Open Anonymity Project
We started this project with the belief that intelligence should be a truly public utility. Like water and electricity, providers should be compensated by usage, not who you are or what you do with it. We think unlinkable inference is a first step towards this “intelligence neutrality”.

clean_title: Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2) speeds up RL for LLMs
summary:
[1/11] Do you really need to finish every rollout in RL for LLM? Not if you make your critic better—and trust it!
We propose Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2): use a learned critic to score chunks of tokens => only need partial rollouts ⇒ train faster than GRPO!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTozGDfbUAAefT8.jpg
────────
[2/11] We show that once critic is accurate, you don’t need to rollout to the end. AC2 replays a prefix of a past trajectory, samples a group of 10k-token action chunks from it, and scores each chunk with the critic. All these updates use no terminal reward.
────────
[3/11] Using GRPO and other variants of PPO in RLVR requires the policy to roll out hundreds of thousands of tokens to get the terminal reward. Critics are sometimes learned, but used only as a baseline.
────────
[4/11] Paper:
Code:
────────
[5/11] Why does AC2 beat GRPO? Two reasons: 25% fewer training steps due to finer grained advantage, and much shorter generations, since most updates only need a 10k-token chunk.
────────
[6/11] Training Qwen3-4B on FineProofs-RL and evaluating on IMO-ProofBench, AC2 reaches GRPO's peak with 2.5x fewer decoding FLOPs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTozWU3agAAVJsO.png
────────
[7/11] The key is knowing when the critic is accurate. AC2 trusts it on a problem only once the critic error becomes small enough. Until then it uses full rollouts and terminal rewards, which also train the critic.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTozRfDaoAAGAXD.jpg
────────
[8/11] More in the paper, including critic diagnostics, ablations, and a version of AC2 that pure actor–critic without groups.
Paper link again:
────────
[9/11] More generally, trusting the critic more and removing the need to rollout all trajectories to completion opens up a largely unexplored part of the LLM RL design space. AC2 is just one example of an algorithm in this space.
────────
[10/11] Policy and critic share weights, and the critic's value is read out with a natural-language prompt. We believe that learning to judge helps learning to act, and vice versa.
────────
[11/11] Huge thanks to my collaborators: @LukeBailey181 (co-lead). @amahankali10 and our advisor @tengyuma !
clean_summary:
Training large language models with reinforcement learning usually means running long rollouts to get terminal rewards, which is slow. Methods like GRPO need hundreds of thousands of tokens per rollout, and critics are often only used as baselines.

Kaiyue Wen proposes AC2, which trusts a learned critic to score chunks of 10,000 tokens instead of full rollouts. Once the critic is accurate enough, AC2 trains faster by using partial rollouts and scoring these chunks, reducing decoding FLOPs by 2.5 times compared to GRPO. The policy and critic share weights, and the critic's value is prompted in natural language. This approach opens new possibilities for RL design in LLMs by relying more on the critic and less on full trajectory rollouts.

Backprop has been the only credit assignment algorithm capable of training large neural nets.
Introducing Dust, the first zeroth-order method to pretrain transformers to approach and sometimes even *exceed* backprop with large amounts of computation (bitter lesson!)
- Dust is on the order of 1,000 to 10,000x more compute efficient than EGGROLL, the state-of-the-art ES method, for training transformers.
- We chose pretraining transformers because it's arguably the hardest task possible for zeroth-order optimization.
- Search in high dimensions is really misunderstood: zeroth-order usually gets better with overparameterization, not worse, i.e. at a fixed population size, larger models (up to 120x) reach a lower loss than smaller ones.
- Backprop-like gradients emerge from a large population of activation perturbations, and the alignment holds up at every scale we tested, up to 1B tokens, which is critical for scaling.
The core idea is a *virtual population*, which helps scale to large populations in transformers by perturbing activations in parallel.

Backpropagation has been the main way to train large neural networks, but it relies on gradient information. Dust is a new method that uses zeroth-order optimization, which doesn’t need gradients, to pretrain transformers. It can match or sometimes beat backprop when given enough computation.

Dust works by creating a virtual population that perturbs activations in parallel, allowing it to scale to large models. Surprisingly, zeroth-order methods like Dust get better with larger models, reaching lower loss with more parameters. It is also 1,000 to 10,000 times more compute efficient than previous zeroth-order methods like EGGROLL. This challenges the idea that gradient-based methods are the only way to train big transformers effectively.

clean_summary:
You might wonder if large language models (LLMs) can come up with truly new research ideas. Kaiyue Wen proposes Priced Guidance, a method that treats predicting a future paper’s idea like a game of 20 Questions. The LLM asks multiple-choice questions about the idea, and each answer costs bits based on how surprising it is. This lets us measure how much information the LLM needs to recover the idea, rather than just guessing until it matches.

Using this approach on 87 recent top papers, Wen finds that models like Fable 5 and Opus 5 compress ideas to under 70 bits, far better than standard compressors. More reasoning doesn’t always help, but combining models does. This compression score also bounds the chance the LLM can generate the idea without hints. Priced Guidance turns idea prediction into a compression problem, opening doors to training better idea generators or estimating rare events.
